sum: - Lululemon is rebuilding its leadership team from the top down after sales fell 4% last quarter.
- On sells running shoes at full price and grew sales 17% last quarter, while Deckers leans on just two brands, HOKA and UGG.
- TJX makes money from other brands' leftover inventory, and Abercrombie keeps adding new places to sell, including Target.

Here's a simple way to think about the following five clothing and shoe companies: They all sell you something to wear, but each one makes its money in a completely different way. That matters more than it sounds. Three of them are each worth roughly $12 billion right now, yet they're in very different spots. When you look at apparel stocks, who the customer is and how the product reaches them tells you more than the logo does.

Lululemon Athletica (NASDAQ: LULU) sells premium leggings and workout clothes through its own 825 stores and its website. That control is great when its products are hot. When they aren't, there's nowhere to hide.

Last quarter, revenue fell 4%, and comparable sales, which track only stores and sites that have been open for at least a year, dropped 9%. Management expects revenue to fall 10% to 11% in the current quarter.

CEO Heidi O'Neill, who spent decades at Nike, took over in September. She is rebuilding the team. In October, she hired away Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be chief product officer, saying the company would put "product, design, and innovation at the center of how we operate." A new brand chief brought in from Four Seasons started Nov. 9. Shares closed at $107.45 on Nov. 11.

Lululemon is known for its high-end yoga and technical apparel, whereas On has built its reputation on innovative running footwear. This comparison explores their financial health and market positioning to determine the better long-term pick.

Lululemon Athletica designs and sells technical athletic apparel, footwear, and accessories through an omni-channel model. It reaches customers via more than 800 company-operated stores and a robust e-commerce platform across multiple countries.

The company also leverages wholesale channels by partnering with fitness studios and university retailers. This diversified approach helps it maintain high brand visibility and reach a loyal customer base in the apparel sector.
In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $11.1 billion, representing revenue growth of approximately 4.9% compared to the prior year. Net income for the period was roughly $1.6 billion.

On develops and distributes premium performance sports products, primarily focusing on its innovative footwear technology. As of the end of 2025, the company operated nearly 70 retail locations worldwide and maintains a strong presence through wholesale partners and its direct-to-consumer e-commerce platform.

Its growth strategy emphasizes global expansion, with a significant retail footprint already established in China. The company relies on its high-performance brand image to attract runners and lifestyle consumers willing to pay a premium price.

Lululemon Athletica (LULU) stock has fallen 74.6% from its highest close since late October 2024, a peak reached on January 30, 2025. This steep decline makes the shares worth a closer look. A yield that high marks either a bargain or a business investors expect to get smaller, so how dependable is the cash behind it?

The retailer generated free cash flow during all 13 twelve-month periods ending between July 2023 and August 2026. Over the twelve months ended August 2, 2026, Lululemon produced $1.35 billion. That figure rose from $1.17 billion a year earlier, although it remained below the level seen two years before.

Shareholders own a slice of that cash whether or not the company pays it out, exactly as they do with profit. Any cash kept inside the business still belongs to its owners. When investors recognize this accumulation, the share price tends to follow, particularly when the cash is growing.

Lululemon generates this cash by selling clothing such as leggings across its 825 stores and digital channel. Over the last twelve months, capital spending took 31.7% of its cash from operations. Free cash flow came to 12.2% of revenue, compared with 4.6% at Nike.

Lululemon’s reported debt consists entirely of lease obligations. That debt rose to $2.14 billion at August 2, 2026, from $1.76 billion a year earlier. Cash and short-term investments cover most of that balance. The remainder equals 6.2% of Lululemon’s market value, leaving a small claim on the cash ahead of shareholders.

The immediate swing factor is whether the new leadership team can translate that plan into cleaner inventories, fewer markdowns and more full price sell through in coming quarters.

The biggest near term risk is that women's leggings softness, tariff pressure and higher costs keep squeezing margins even if revenue stabilises. Two long-tenured executives are leaving, two new roles were filled from outside, and searches are still open for a chief brand officer and chief technology officer. This shows some uncertainty from the top, and markets typically price in uncertainty before they price results.

items.t: Bear of the Day: Lululemon athletica (LULU)
sum: Anyone who regularly follows my Bear of the Day reports will notice that apparel companies appear frequently. While certain brands enjoy periods of exceptional growth and market leadership, most eventually confront the industry's inherent challenges: rapidly shifting trends, evolving consumer preferences, intense competition, and difficult inventory management.

Lululemon athletica (LULU), once among the premier growth stories in apparel, has been unable to escape that cycle. Growth has decelerated sharply, competition in premium athleisure has intensified, and the stock has suffered accordingly. Falling earnings estimates have pushed LULU to a Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell).

Bulls will point to the valuation, and the stock does screen inexpensive after its decline. But a cheap multiple built on falling estimates is a moving target. Every downward revision quietly raises the forward P/E on the same share price, which is how a stock that looks like a bargain keeps getting cheaper. Valuation only becomes an argument once estimates stop falling.

The brand is not dead, and Lululemon products remain widely worn. But brand recognition alone does not support a multiple. Until growth reaccelerates and estimates stabilize, investors have little reason to step in.

Analysts have near-unanimously slashed the profit outlook across every timeline. Current quarter earnings estimates have been cut 34.4%, while current year estimates are down 10.8% and next year more than 13%.

Sales growth is languishing as well, with current year revenue projected to fall 0.2% and next year expected to see only a modest 3.2% bump. Earnings are expected to drop 17.5% this year before a tepid 5.5% rebound next year.

The recent quarter highlights the major challenges facing the business. Revenue rose 4% to $2.5 billion, but comparable sales actually fell 2% and in the core North America market, comps dropped 6%. Gross margin contracted 410 basis points on tariffs and fixed-cost deleverage, with second quarter operating margin now guided to roughly 11.6% versus 20.7% a year ago. Management also cut full year EPS guidance by more than a dollar to $10.95–$11.15, blaming negative brand commentary on social channels and product launches that failed to land.

The activewear giant arranged a large-scale promotional event on a section of the Great Wall of China near Beijing in late May, complete with thousands of attendees, Chinese celebrities, and what was meant to be a traditional drum performance. The trouble is that the drum used reportedly wasn't Chinese at all. It was Japanese, and Chinese social media has not been gentle about it.

The backlash on the Chinese social media platform Weibo has been substantial, with the related discussion topping tens of millions of views, and the company forced to issue an apology. Considering that China has been one of the most important growth markets for Lululemon over the past few years, this is the absolute last thing the stock needed. The shares were already deep in the doghouse, and a public misstep like this only deepens the sense that everything that could be going wrong for Lululemon is.
However, for those who can step back and look at the bigger picture, this might be exactly the kind of moment that long-term bulls will look back on with a wry smile.

This latest gaffe in China didn't cause the selloff in Lululemon, but it has added to one that's been quietly grinding away since late 2023. Shares are down close to 50% year to date, having hit a fresh low earlier this month, and are trading at roughly the same level as eight years ago.

sum: Shares of Lululemon Athletica Inc. dropped about 13 percent on Thursday on news of the appointment of former Nike veteran Heidi O’Neill as CEO. Analysts were mixed on the surprise choice, with some lamenting her lack of experience as a CEO and with turnarounds. Some felt Nike’s recent struggles have stained her reputation. The fact that O’Neill’s start date isn’t until September will also delay her making any impact.

O’Neill, who will take over as CEO on September 8 due to a non-compete clause with Nike, succeeds Calvin McDonald, who stepped down, effective January 31, after seven years as CEO amid slowing North American growth and pressure from Lululemon founder and major shareholder, Chip Wilson, and activist investor Elliott Investment Management.
O’Neill, 61, resigned from Nike in May 2025 after a 27-year career at the company.

She most recently served as the company’s president of Consumer, Product & Brand, where she led the global product engine (across all regions, including North America, China, EMEA, and APLA). In particular, O’Neill was credited over the years with helping grow Nike’s presence with women, Lululemon’s core consumer.

Marti Morfitt, executive chair of Lululemon’s Board of Directors, in a release announcing to appointment, said, “We selected Heidi because of the breadth of her experience, her demonstrated success in delivering breakthrough ideas and initiatives at scale, and her ability to be a knowledgeable change and growth agent.”

The hiring comes as activist investor Elliott Investment Management, which has built a roughly $1 billion investment in Lululemon, late last year suggested Lululemon hire Jane Nielsen, who helped orchestrate a turnaround at Ralph Lauren as COO and CFO, as CEO and some analysts endorsed the choice. She was also the former CFO at Coach.

Needham & Co.’s Tom Nikic, who has a “Hold” on Lululemon’s shares, believes the negative reaction from the stock market is in large part because Lululemon didn’t choose Nielsen, who he said is “very highly regarded” by investors.

sum: Lululemon founder-turned-activist Chip Wilson is trying to excise private equity firm Advent from the beleaguered athletic apparel company’s board as part of an ongoing proxy fight.

Wilson, who quit Lululemon’s board in 2015 but remains the company’s second-biggest shareholder, launched a proxy war late last year in a bid to remake the board while it looked for a new CEO. While Wilson has said he doesn’t want a board seat for himself, he is making it clear that he will not consider any settlement with the company unless two legacy Advent-linked directors, including David Mussafer, resign, according to people familiar with Wilson’s thinking.

Advent has had a long and successful relationship with Lululemon and Wilson. It was a partnership that helped Lululemon go public, made Wilson one of Canada’s wealthiest businessmen, and minted billions for both parties.

But Wilson has soured on Advent in recent years, and now views the private equity firm’s influence and lingering presence as a personification of Lululemon’s ailments. He lays Lululemon’s “loss of cool,” as Wilson wrote in a WSJ ad last year, at the feet of Mussafer’s focus on appeasing Wall Street analysts rather than thinking ahead about what customers will want to wear, the people close to him say.

Wilson has singled out the continuing presence of Advent managing partner David Mussafer, who is Lululemon’s lead independent director, and Lululemon chair Marti Morfitt, as making any settlement deal impossible, those people said. Mussafer took his seat as part of a deal Advent struck with the company more than a decade ago; Morfitt, while not formally affiliated with Advent, was brought onto the board of another Advent portfolio company and is seen by Wilson as working in lockstep with Mussafer. (The separation of Lululemon’s board chair and lead independent roles itself is a legacy of that deal Advent struck.)

Wilson’s frustrations are compounded by Advent’s spotty record in the consumer space, the people say ; another Advent name, the haircare brand Olaplex, has seen its stock collapse since its 2022 IPO. (Mussafer and two other Lululemon directors are also on Olaplex’s board.)
Advent has had some wins in the space, including a highly-lucrative, $2.7 billion deal for the maker of Rao’s pasta sauces.

lululemon's investment case is fundamentally driven by its premium market leadership and sustained share gains within the global athletic apparel industry. The company holds the first position in women's activewear in the United States and has built a meaningful global footprint across more than 30 geographies, with China emerging as its second-largest market.

Over the past several years, lululemon has significantly expanded its revenue base and global relevance, positioning itself as a leading player within the consumer discretionary landscape, supported by strong brand loyalty and pricing power. Its digital channel now represents a substantial portion of total sales, reinforcing lululemon's influence across both physical and online retail ecosystems.

lululemon is strengthening its competitive moat through a disciplined three-pillar operating model focused on product creation, product activation and enterprise efficiency. Management is reenergizing the product portfolio by increasing new-style penetration to 35%, accelerating design cycles and emphasizing innovation in performance-led categories such as run, train and outerwear.

sum: Lululemon Athletica stock (ISIN CA5500211090) is trading below recent analyst price targets ahead of the company’s second-quarter fiscal 2026 earnings report scheduled for September 3, 2026, with Wall Street expecting a sharp year-over-year decline in profit alongside slightly lower sales. Recent analyst commentary highlights that the shares change hands at $118.83 and have fallen more than 40% year-to-date as of August 31, 2026, while the consensus calls for earnings of $1.79 per share on revenue of $2.47 billion in the upcoming quarter.

Expectations for Lululemon’s second quarter of fiscal 2026 are muted, with the earnings consensus pointing to a significant profit contraction versus the prior year. According to a Q2 2026 earnings preview, Wall Street projects quarterly earnings of $1.79 per share, which would represent a 42.3% decline compared with the same quarter a year earlier.

Revenue is also forecast to soften modestly. The same consensus calls for sales of $2.47 billion in Q2 2026, a 2.3% decrease year-over-year, signaling that slower growth in key markets could be weighing on Lululemon’s top line even before any cost pressures are considered. This combination of lower expected revenue and sharply lower earnings underscores investor concerns that the company may be entering a tougher phase of its growth story.

For investors, the magnitude of that expected profit decline is crucial. A 42.3% drop in earnings on only a 2.3% revenue decline implies significant margin compression compared with last year’s quarter, and the upcoming report will show whether higher costs, weaker demand, or a mix of both is responsible for the pressure.
Recent rating calls and price targets frame valuation debate

Despite the drawdown in the share price, several analyst houses have maintained neutral stances with modestly supportive price targets. One recent note reaffirmed a Hold rating on Lululemon with a price target of $115, while another maintained a Neutral view and a $110 target as of September 1, 2026, citing caution around brand momentum and macro headwinds in major markets. A German-language analyst summary reports that the stock most recently traded at $120.26 compared with those $115 and $110 targets.

sum: Lululemon stock price has had another bad year as it crashed by 45%, even as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 indices jumped to record highs. It has dropped from the all-time high of $516 in December 2023 to the current $207, bringing its market cap from $68 billion to $25 billion. So, will the stock rebound in 2026?
Lululemon Athletica, one of the top beneficiaries of the Covid-19 pandemic, has become a fallen angel as its growth momentum has slowed.
Its annual revenue growth stood at 42% in 2021, 30% in 2022, 18.6% in 2023, and 10% last year. Its trailing twelve-month (TTM) revenue growth stood at 8.7%.

The most recent results showed that the revenue rose by 7% in the third quarter to $2.6 billion. This revenue was driven by its international segment, whose revenue rose by 33%. Its Americas revenue dropped by 2%.

The company’s comparable sales in the Americas segment dropped by 5%, while in the international market rose by 18%. This growth was driven by China, a country that has become one of its important markets.
Lululemon’s growth slowdown is partly because of the rising competition from other companies like Nike, Adidas, Gap, Vuori, and Sweaty Betty, which have taken market share from its company.

At the same time, Donald Trump’s tariffs have not helped as the company makes most of its products in Asia. In its most recent results, the company announced that its income from operations would receive a $210 million hit from tariffs.

items.t: Lululemon CEO McDonald to step down, shares rise 10%
Lululemon CEO Calvin McDonald to depart in January as retailer struggles to compete, woo shoppers
sum: Lululemon shares jumped more than 9% on Friday, after the company announced its CEO Calvin McDonald will step down.
McDonald's departure, effective Jan. 31, follows more than a year of underperformance at the athleisure company.
Lululemon's board of directors is working with a "leading executive search firm" to identify its next CEO, it said in a news release. McDonald will stay on as a senior advisor through March 31.

"The timing is right for a change," McDonald said on a call with analysts, "I've described being CEO of Lululemon as my dream job. It truly has lived up to every expectation and given me the opportunity of a lifetime."

Lululemon's CFO Meghan Frank and Chief Commercial Officer André Maestrini will serve as interim co-CEOs during the search process. The company's board chair Marti Morfitt will also take on the expanded role of executive chair. In a statement, she said the company has a strong foundation in place but needs a new leader that can guide it through a transition.

"As we look to the future, the Board is focused on identifying a leader with a track record of driving companies through periods of growth and transformation to guide the company's next chapter of success," said Morfitt.

The leadership change follows more than a year of underperformance at Lululemon and calls for change from its founder and its largest independent shareholder Chip Wilson. Two months ago, he took out a full page ad in the Wall Street Journal saying the company is "in a nosedive" and it needed to "stop chasing Wall Street at the expense of customers."
